definitions.definition: A fast electronic machine that accepts digitised input, processes it by a list of internally stored instructions and produces output information.
The five independent parts of a digital computer: input, output, memory unit, arithmetic and logic unit, and control unit.
Symbolic notation used to describe the microoperation transfers among registers.
A group of wires forming a path over which information moves from any of several sources to any of several destinations.
Special register that holds the address of the memory word being accessed, set before the memory is read or written.
An elementary operation on binary data held in registers, of four kinds: register transfer, arithmetic, logic and shift.
Bit-wise operations on strings of bits held in registers, useful for manipulating binary data and making decisions from bit values.
Operation in which each 1 in a second register forces the matching bit of the first register to 1, leaving other bits unchanged.
Operation in which each 1 in a second register inverts the matching bit of the first register, leaving other bits unchanged.
Operation in which each 0 in a second register clears the matching bit of the first register to 0, leaving other bits unchanged.
Operation that introduces a specific bit pattern into a register while leaving the other bit positions unchanged.
Shift in which the serial input bit fed into the register is always zero.
Shift in which the bit shifted out at one end of the register is fed back as the serial input at the other end.
Shift meant for signed binary numbers that keeps the sign of the number unchanged while performing multiplication or division.
A group of bits that tells the computer to perform a specific operation, made up of a sequence of microoperations.
The part of an instruction that specifies the operation to be performed.
Processor part that translates machine instructions into the control signals for the microoperations that implement them.
Control unit implementation made up of sequential and combinational circuits that generate the control signals.
Repeating sequence of fetching an instruction, decoding it, reading any indirect effective address and executing it before starting again.
Request raised by an interface when its device is ready, making the CPU branch to a service routine and then return to its task.
Storage accessed in last-in first-out order through a pointer, on which only push and pop operations are applicable.
Postfix way of writing arithmetic expressions, with operators after operands and no parentheses, that suits stack-based evaluation.
Rule for interpreting or modifying the address field of an instruction before the operand is actually referenced.
Mode in which the operand addresses are specified implicitly in the definition of the instruction itself.
Mode in which the operand itself is given in the instruction instead of its address, so the operand is fast to acquire.
Mode in which the instruction names a register that holds the memory address of the operand, saving instruction bits.
Mode in which the address field of the instruction gives the physical memory address used directly for the operand.
Mode in which the address field points to a memory location that contains the operand address, needing an extra memory access.
Mode that forms the operand address by adding the address field of the instruction to the contents of an index register.
Request raised from outside the CPU and memory, such as an I/O transfer request, timeout or power failure.
Request caused by the program currently running, such as stack overflow, divide by zero, op-code violation or protection violation.
Request initiated by executing an instruction, for example a supervisor call that switches from user mode to supervisor mode.
Processor design with a large instruction set of 100-250 instructions, many addressing modes, variable-length formats and instructions that manipulate memory operands.
Processor design with few instructions and addressing modes, memory access only by load and store, fixed-length single-cycle instructions and hardwired control.
Program stored in memory that generates all the control signals required to execute the instruction set correctly.
Control-memory entry holding a control word with all control information for one clock cycle and a sequencing word giving the next address.
Control store whose contents can be modified, so the microprogram and even the instruction set can be changed.
Microprogram control unit that determines the microinstruction address to be executed in the next clock cycle.
Mapping from the op-code of an instruction to the address of the first microinstruction of its routine, implemented by ROM or PLA.
Number system that uses r distinct digit symbols, where each digit is multiplied by an integer power of r.
Result of subtracting an n-digit number N from rⁿ, where r is the base.
Result of subtracting an n-digit number N from rⁿ − 1, where r is the base.
Scheme in which the binary point always sits in one position, so the stored number is treated as a fraction or an integer.
Scheme storing a number as a mantissa times a radix raised to an exponent, widening the range a register can hold.
Floating-point number whose mantissa has a nonzero most significant digit; the number zero cannot be put in this form.
Shifting one mantissa while adjusting its exponent until both exponents are equal, needed before adding or subtracting floating-point numbers.
Condition in which an addition result needs more digits than the register holds, detected when the last two carries differ.
Multiplication method that subtracts the multiplicand at the first 1 of a string of 1s in the multiplier and adds it after the string.
Path for information transfers between the CPU and the main memory.
Path for information transfers between the CPU and input-output devices through their interfaces.
Transfer between two independent units that requires control signals to indicate the time at which data is being sent.
Pulse supplied by one unit to tell the other unit when a transfer is to occur.
Transfer method in which a control signal accompanies each data item, so the transfer rate follows the slower unit.
Character-by-character transmission in which each character is framed by a start bit of 0, data bits and stop bits, with the idle line at 1.
Transfer mode in which the interface requests service when its device is ready, and the CPU pauses its task to run a service routine.
Mechanism deciding which request is served first when several arrive together and which may break in while another is being serviced.
Interface that lets data move directly between an I/O device and memory without passing through the CPU.
Organisation of memory levels meant to obtain the highest possible access speed while minimising the total cost of the memory system.
Fast, small-capacity memory that holds the information most likely to be accessed.
Tendency of programs to reuse recently used information, as in loops, and to access words adjacent to those just accessed.
Cache write policy that updates both the cache and main memory in parallel when the word is found in the cache.
Fixed-size group of words into which the address space and the memory space are each divided.
Execution of concurrent events in the computing process to achieve faster computational speed.
Architectural classification of parallel computers by the number of instruction streams and data streams, each single or multiple.
Sequence of instructions read from memory, one of the two stream types used in Flynn's classification.
Pipeline conflict that occurs when hardware resources needed by overlapped instructions cannot be provided, as with a single memory port.
Pipeline conflict that occurs when the execution of an instruction depends on the result of a previous instruction not yet available.
Pipeline delay caused by branches and other instructions that change the program counter, which postpone fetching the next instruction.
Data path that routes a value from its source, usually an ALU, straight to a user, bypassing a designated register.
Associative memory whose entries hold addresses of earlier branches with their target instruction and the next few instructions.
High-speed register file that stores an entire loop so it can execute without accessing memory.
Guessing the branch condition and fetching an instruction stream based on the guess, so a correct guess removes the branch penalty.
Hardware action that detects a hazard and stalls the pipeline until the hazard is cleared.
Interconnection of two or more CPUs with memory and I/O equipment.
Several computers connected together by means of communication lines.
Non-blocking switch with crosspoints at the intersections of processor buses and memory module paths, giving a separate path to each module.
High-speed network made of successive switching stages, with processing elements on one end and memory elements on the other.
Multistage network of 2×2 switching elements joined by perfect shuffle, with exactly one path from each source to each destination.
Loosely coupled structure of 2ⁿ processors joined as an n-dimensional binary cube, each directly linked to n neighbours.
